This modulo 2 VQLS is inherently free from singularity. It is adapt to stabilizer coding theory and may find applications in areas such as decoders and the design of quantum gate sequences. Therefore, our work demonstrates the practical potential of VQLS in quantum computing, providing a solid experimental foundation and methodological guidance for its real-world applications.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally validates a generalized variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) on a photonic computing platform, solving 4D linear systems in complex and finite fields. It handles ill-conditioned problems via Tikhonov-inspired perturbation and extends VQLS to finite field F2 with modulo 2 constraints for singularity-free operation, with applications in stabilizer coding theory.
AI.motivation: To experimentally validate a generalized VQLS on a photonic platform, addressing practical challenges like ill-conditioned (singular) systems and extending the solver to finite field F2 for applications in coding theory and quantum gate design.
AI.method: The authors implement a generalized VQLS on a photonic computing platform, solving 4D linear systems. For singular/ill-conditioned problems in complex fields, they introduce perturbation terms inspired by Tikhonov regularization. For finite field F2, they redesign the cost function with modulo 2 operations and impose constraints on the solution vector.
AI.result: The generalized VQLS successfully solves non-singular and ill-conditioned systems in the complex field using perturbation regularization. The modulo 2 VQLS is inherently singularity-free and adapted to stabilizer coding theory.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the practical potential of VQLS in quantum computing, providing experimental validation and methodological guidance for real-world applications including decoders and quantum gate sequence design.

title: Syndrome-as-Header: A Quantum Label-Switching Architecture via Uncorrectable Error Injection
summary: Scaling quantum networks beyond point-to-point links requires packet forwarding that can tolerate control-plane timing uncertainty. Existing optical-burst switching (OBS) and quantum-wrapper-based packet switching (QW) rely on external classical headers whose jitter-prone processing must remain aligned with in-flight quantum payloads, creating guard-window or fiber-delay-line budget failures. This paper proposes Syndrome-as-Header (SAH), a quantum label-switching architecture that embeds routing labels into the syndrome structure of an encoded payload. The proposed scheme uses Uncorrectable Error Injection (UEI) to map flow labels to reference syndromes and builds a syndrome-space header codebook whose decoding regions remain distinguishable under correctable channel-induced syndrome deviations. Core routers extract the syndrome header, suppress the correctable residual channel-error component, and swap labels without measuring or decoding the logical payload. SAH supports FAST forwarding and VERIFICATION mode, the latter providing end-to-end consistency checking while retaining swappable labels. In NSFNet timing benchmarks with common per-hop quantum error correction (QEC), SAH eliminates the external-header/payload alignment condition, so timing uncertainty appears as memory residence and delivered latency rather than alignment-budget drops. With a $T_2$-based memory-residence penalty, the advantage depends on router memory coherence; for sufficiently long coherence, SAH maintains higher acceptance and throughput than OBS+QEC and QW+QEC under high jitter.

AI.tldr: Syndrome-as-Header (SAH) is a quantum label-switching architecture that embeds routing labels into the syndrome structure of encoded quantum payloads, eliminating the need for external-header/payload alignment and improving tolerance to timing jitter in quantum networks.
AI.motivation: Scaling quantum networks beyond point-to-point links requires packet forwarding that tolerates control-plane timing uncertainty; existing OBS and QW approaches suffer from guard-window or fiber-delay-line budget failures due to jitter-prone external header processing that must remain aligned with in-flight quantum payloads.
AI.method: SAH uses Uncorrectable Error Injection (UEI) to map flow labels to reference syndromes, building a syndrome-space header codebook with distinguishable decoding regions under correctable channel-induced syndrome deviations. Core routers extract the syndrome header, suppress correctable residual errors, and swap labels without measuring or decoding the logical payload. Two modes: FAST forwarding and VERIFICATION (end-to-end consistency checking).
AI.result: In NSFNet timing benchmarks with per-hop QEC, SAH eliminates the external-header/payload alignment condition, so timing uncertainty appears as memory residence and delivered latency rather than alignment-budget drops. With a T2-based memory-residence penalty, SAH maintains higher acceptance and throughput than OBS+QEC and QW+QEC under high jitter when router memory coherence is sufficiently long.
AI.conclusion: SAH provides a viable quantum label-switching architecture that removes alignment constraints, enabling more robust quantum network scaling under timing uncertainty, with advantages depending on router memory coherence time.

title: Geometric Mode Steering of the Quantum Mpemba Effect
summary: The slowest Liouvillian mode often bottlenecks the relaxation of an open quantum system to its steady state. Standard strategies circumvent this bottleneck by selecting special initial states or engineering the dissipator. Here we show that neither is necessary. We introduce a pre-dissipative geometric steering protocol that reshapes any given pure or mixed state before relaxation begins -- coherent rotations interleaved with nonselective projective measurements -- at fixed Lindblad generator. By steering the state's Bloch direction along geodesic paths, the protocol suppresses its overlap with the slowest Liouvillian modes. The prepared state then starts farther from equilibrium yet relaxes faster, realizing the quantum Mpemba effect, whenever two computable conditions hold: reduced slow-mode overlap and a larger initial distance to stationarity. Our framework treats real and complex spectral gaps uniformly, and we demonstrate robust Mpemba acceleration in driven qubit and multiqubit systems using operations available in trapped-ion and superconducting platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a pre-dissipative geometric steering protocol using coherent rotations and nonselective projective measurements that reshapes quantum states before relaxation begins, suppressing overlap with slow Liouvillian modes to achieve faster relaxation (quantum Mpemba effect) without requiring special initial states or modifying the dissipator.
AI.motivation: The slowest Liouvillian mode bottlenecks relaxation to steady state in open quantum systems. Standard approaches require either special initial states or engineered dissipators; the authors aim to circumvent this bottleneck without either constraint.
AI.method: A pre-dissipative geometric steering protocol that interleaves coherent rotations with nonselective projective measurements to steer the Bloch direction along geodesic paths, suppressing overlap with the slowest Liouvillian eigenmodes before relaxation begins, while keeping the Lindblad generator fixed.
AI.result: The protocol realizes the quantum Mpemba effect (starting farther from equilibrium yet relaxing faster) when two conditions hold: reduced slow-mode overlap and a larger initial distance to stationarity. Demonstrates robust acceleration in driven qubit and multiqubit systems using operations available in trapped-ion and superconducting platforms, treating real and complex spectral gaps uniformly.
AI.conclusion: Neither special initial states nor engineered dissipators are necessary to accelerate relaxation; pre-dissipative geometric steering alone suffices, providing a practical framework for quantum Mpemba acceleration in current quantum platforms.

title: Structure-Aware Variational State Preparation for Quantum Basket Option Pricing
summary: Basket option pricing often relies on Monte Carlo estimation, for which quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) provides a quadratic speed-up. However, the practical benefit of QAE can be limited by the depth of the state-preparation circuit. We propose a structure-aware quantum state-preparation framework for QAE-based basket option pricing. The framework uses tensor-train (TT) rank information to design shallow variational state-preparation circuits. In the independent regime, TT ranks remove unnecessary entangling links from a hardware-efficient ansatz. In correlated basket settings, we instead prepare asset-wise marginals locally and train a compact latent block to match the basket cumulative distribution function. The Basket-CDF objective targets the basket pushforward distribution rather than the full joint state, directly aligning state preparation with basket-dependent payoffs. Numerical experiments show that the proposed circuits replace the exponential state-preparation depth scaling of exact amplitude loading with linear scaling, while maintaining low-percent basket-pricing errors. Additional sampling-based training experiments and an end-to-end QAE integration study support compatibility with sample-estimated training and standard QAE-based pricing workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a tensor-train rank-informed quantum state-preparation framework for QAE-based basket option pricing that replaces exponential depth scaling with linear scaling while maintaining low pricing errors.
AI.motivation: Basket option pricing via QAE offers quadratic speed-up but is practically limited by the depth of state-preparation circuits, motivating the need for shallower circuit designs.
AI.method: The framework uses tensor-train (TT) rank information to design shallow variational state-preparation circuits. For independent assets, TT ranks remove unnecessary entangling links from hardware-efficient ansatz. For correlated baskets, asset-wise marginals are prepared locally and a compact latent block is trained to match the basket cumulative distribution function (CDF), targeting the basket pushforward distribution rather than the full joint state.
AI.result: The proposed circuits replace exponential state-preparation depth scaling with linear scaling while maintaining low-percent basket-pricing errors. Additional experiments confirm compatibility with sample-estimated training and standard QAE-based pricing workflows.
AI.conclusion: A structure-aware quantum state-preparation approach using TT ranks enables practical, shallow-depth QAE-based basket option pricing with favorable scaling and accuracy trade-offs.

title: No Finite NPA Level Characterizes the Complete Quantum Set in the Simplest Bell Scenario
comment: Submitted to Physical Review Letters on 14 July 2026. Closely overlapping preprints arXiv:2607.13762 and arXiv:2607.13774 appeared on 15 July 2026. This work was completed independently beforehand and gives a distinct fully analytical proof with broader behavior-set consequences
summary: The Navascués--Pironio--Acín (NPA) hierarchy gives the standard semidefinite outer approximations to quantum behaviors. Whether \emph{any} finite level can already equal the quantum set has remained open even in the bipartite scenario with two binary measurements per party. We demonstrate that \emph{no finite level} is exact. For the symmetric doubly tilted CHSH functional $h_α=A_0B_0+A_0B_1+A_1B_0-A_1B_1+α(A_0+B_0)$, set $T=1-α$. Its quantum maximum satisfies $[ω_{\rm Q}(1-T)-(4-2T)]/T^3\to4/3$, whereas every fixed NPA level satisfies $[ω_L(1-T)-ω_{\rm Q}(1-T)]/T^3\to+\infty$. Under the corresponding boundary rescaling, an explicit expectation of the positive operator $ω_{\rm Q}(1-t^2)I-H_t$ converges to the Motzkin polynomial. A bounded fixed-level error would therefore make the Motzkin polynomial plus a nonnegative constant a sum of squares, which is impossible. Consequently, every standard NPA relaxation based on a fixed finite list of words in the measurement projectors strictly contains the complete quantum set, and its nonquantum behaviors accumulate at a local deterministic behavior. Thus, the finite-level exactness of CHSH and all one-sided tilted CHSH maxima does not extend to an exact finite-level description of the complete quantum set in the minimal scenario.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that no finite level of the NPA hierarchy exactly captures the quantum set, even in the minimal bipartite scenario (two parties, two binary measurements each). Using the symmetric doubly tilted CHSH functional, they show that the quantum maximum converges smoothly while any fixed NPA level diverges, implying finite-level relaxations always contain nonquantum behaviors that accumulate at deterministic points.
AI.motivation: Whether any finite level of the NPA hierarchy can exactly equal the quantum set has remained an open problem, even in the simplest bipartite scenario with two binary measurements per party. This work aims to resolve this fundamental question.
AI.method: The authors analyze the symmetric doubly tilted CHSH functional $h_α$ and study the asymptotic behavior of its quantum maximum $ω_Q$ versus the maximum $ω_L$ from a fixed finite NPA level as $α\to1$ (or $T=1-α\to0$). They rescale the boundary and examine the convergence of an explicit operator expectation to the Motzkin polynomial, which is a known polynomial that is not a sum of squares.
AI.result: The quantum maximum satisfies $[ω_Q(1-T)-(4-2T)]/T^3\to4/3$, while every fixed NPA level satisfies $[ω_L(1-T)-ω_Q(1-T)]/T^3\to+\infty$. Under boundary rescaling, an expectation converges to the Motzkin polynomial. If a finite NPA level were exact, the Motzkin polynomial plus a nonnegative constant would be a sum of squares, which is impossible.
AI.conclusion: No finite level of the NPA hierarchy is exact; every finite-level relaxation strictly contains the quantum set, and nonquantum behaviors accumulate at a local deterministic point. Finite-level exactness of CHSH and one-sided tilted CHSH does not extend to an exact finite-level description of the full quantum set.

title: Exact No Signaling in Time without Temporal Classicality
summary: No signaling in time (NSIT) has often been treated as the clean operational remnant of noninvasive measurability. If an earlier measurement leaves every later marginal unchanged, the temporal process appears classical. We show that this inference is false. We introduce common fixed points (CFPs) of nonselective measurement channels as an exact mechanism that erases all marginal evidence of invasiveness while preserving disturbed outcome conditioned branches. For a qutrit ring subject to a local degenerate Luders measurement, we solve the full CFP manifold analytically. Every state on this manifold satisfies exact pairwise NSIT, yet every nontrivial member violates a Leggett Garg inequality, including the maximally mixed state. The violation is governed by finite branch displacement, not by residual signaling. Hidden variable reconstruction, entropic witnesses, protocol landscape scans, noise robustness, and finite shot simulations show that exact NSIT certifies only the disappearance of marginal signals after outcome erasure, not the existence of a classical temporal history.

AI.tldr: NSIT (no signaling in time) signatures alone cannot certify classical temporal processes. Common fixed points of nonselective measurement channels can erase all marginal evidence of invasiveness while preserving quantum correlations, as shown in a qutrit ring with a local degenerate Luders measurement. The maximally mixed state violates a Leggett-Garg inequality despite satisfying exact pairwise NSIT.
AI.motivation: To challenge the widely held assumption that no signaling in time (NSIT) conditions imply classical, noninvasive measurability in temporal processes.
AI.method: Introduction of common fixed points (CFPs) of nonselective measurement channels as a mechanism explaining how NSIT can hold while quantum invasiveness remains. Analytical solution of the full CFP manifold for a qutrit ring with a local degenerate Luders measurement, verified with hidden variable reconstruction, entropic witnesses, noise robustness, and finite shot simulations.
AI.result: Every state on the CFP manifold satisfies exact pairwise NSIT, yet nontrivial members (including the maximally mixed state) violate Leggett-Garg inequalities. The violation is governed by finite branch displacement, not residual signaling.
AI.conclusion: Exact NSIT does not certify the existence of a classical temporal history; it only certifies the disappearance of marginal signals after outcome erasure.

title: Adaptive Entanglement Management in Quantum Multi-Core Architectures
summary: Scalable quantum computing architectures increasingly rely on multi-core designs, where qubits are distributed across multiple processing cores interconnected through a quantum Network-on-Chip (NoC). In such systems, inter-core communication is typically realized through entanglement-assisted quantum teleportation, making efficient entanglement generation critical for performance. In this paper, we perform a comparative study of three entanglement management paradigms for multi-core quantum processors: reactive on-demand generation (ODG), proactive continuous pre-generation (CGP), and an adaptive continuous pre-generation approach (ACGP). While ODG generates entanglement only when required, CGP reduces average teleportation latency by pre-generating EPR pairs in the background. To improve upon this, we propose ACGP which dynamically adjusts entanglement generation probabilities based on observed inter-core communication patterns. We evaluate these approaches using an extended SeQUeNCe simulator on mesh-based multi-core architectures on real benchmark circuits. Results show that ACGP significantly reduces average teleportation latency compared to ODG and CGP. Although pre-generation introduces fidelity degradation due to storage time, entanglement purification effectively restores fidelity with minimal impact on latency. These results demonstrate that adaptive entanglement managements can substantially improve communication efficiency in scalable quantum multi-core systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes and evaluates an adaptive continuous pre-generation approach (ACGP) for entanglement management in multi-core quantum processors, showing significant teleportation latency reduction over reactive and static proactive approaches.
AI.motivation: Multi-core quantum processors require efficient inter-core communication via entanglement-assisted quantum teleportation, making entanglement generation critical for performance.
AI.method: Comparative study of three entanglement management paradigms (ODG, CGP, ACGP) evaluated using an extended SeQUeNCe simulator on mesh-based multi-core architectures with real benchmark circuits.
AI.result: ACGP significantly reduces average teleportation latency compared to ODG and CGP; pre-generation fidelity degradation is effectively restored by entanglement purification with minimal latency impact.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive entanglement management (ACGP) can substantially improve communication efficiency in scalable quantum multi-core systems, with entanglement purification effectively restoring fidelity with minimal latency impact.

title: Emergence and Recovery of (logical) Kochen-Specker Contextuality via Hamilton Extension
summary: Logical Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality is widely regarded as an intrinsic property of specially constructed measurement configurations. We show instead that it can emerge from KS-colorable vector sets through a constructive procedure we call the Hamilton extension. Defined for four-dimensional vector sets, the Hamilton extension associates each real vector with a measurement context while inducing additional measurement contexts among Hamilton-extended children of distinct parent vectors. These emergent contexts fundamentally alter the compatibility structure, transforming KS-colorable configurations into KS-uncolorable ones and recovering logical contextuality lost under apex-vertex augmentation. We establish a sharp and optimal threshold -- the Hamilton extension of every five-vector parent set remains KS-colorable, whereas suitably chosen six-vector parent sets already generate logical KS contradictions. Thus, six vectors constitute the smallest parent set capable of generating KS contradiction through this mechanism. Our results reveal a new structural route to contextuality, provide a systematic framework for constructing compact KS sets, and have implications for contextuality-based quantum information protocols and graph-theoretic approaches to nonclassicality.

AI.tldr: Logical Kochen-Specker contextuality can emerge from KS-colorable vector sets via a constructive Hamilton extension procedure; six vectors are the minimum parent set size to generate KS contradictions through this mechanism.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing view that logical KS contextuality is an intrinsic property of specially constructed measurement configurations, and to show it can emerge from KS-colorable vector sets via a systematic constructive procedure.
AI.method: The Hamilton extension: a constructive procedure for four-dimensional vector sets that associates each real vector with a measurement context and induces additional contexts among Hamilton-extended children of distinct parent vectors, transforming the compatibility structure.
AI.result: The Hamilton extension of every five-vector parent set remains KS-colorable, while suitably chosen six-vector parent sets already generate logical KS contradictions, establishing six vectors as the smallest generating set.
AI.conclusion: Reveals a new structural route to contextuality, provides a systematic framework for constructing compact KS sets, and has implications for contextuality-based quantum information protocols and graph-theoretic approaches to nonclassicality.

title: Worst-Case Quantum Algorithm for Optimal Polynomial Intersection Beyond Decoded Quantum Interferometry
summary:
The Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem asks us to find a low-degree polynomial over a finite field whose values lie in prescribed subsets on as many given inputs as possible. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) gives a quantum algorithm for OPI in parameter regimes beyond those achieved by the best known classical heuristics. Follow-up works improve the parameter regimes, but their analyses are limited to average-case settings. Recently, Sun and Wootters showed that, even in the worst case, OPI has a solution in a larger parameter regime than the one covered by DQI. However, they left open whether one can design a quantum algorithm that solves OPI in the worst-case beyond the DQI regime.
  We give such a quantum algorithm. As a byproduct, we also improve the existential bound of Sun and Wootters in certain parameter regimes. In particular, when each subset contains roughly half of the field elements, our algorithm finds a solution with satisfaction rate $s=1$ whenever the rate satisfies $R>0.75$. This matches the previous average-case bound, whereas DQI cannot achieve $s=1$ unless $R=1$. Our existential bound guarantees the existence of a solution when $R> 0.7158$, improving over the previous threshold $R>0.7495$. More generally, our existential results extend to the Max-LINSAT problem with respect to arbitrary maximum distance separable (MDS) codes. The corresponding algorithmic results apply only to MDS codes whose dual admits an efficient list decoder. Our results are obtained through a novel application of a Brascamp--Lieb-type inequality in the MDS setting, which may have further applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum algorithm solving the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem in worst-case settings beyond the DQI regime, improves existential bounds from R>0.7495 to R>0.7158, achieves satisfaction rate s=1 when R>0.75 (matching average-case bound), and extends results to Max-LINSAT with MDS codes via a novel Brascamp–Lieb-type inequality.
AI.motivation: Sun and Wootters showed worst-case OPI solutions exist beyond DQI regimes but left open whether a quantum algorithm could achieve this. The paper aims to design such a quantum algorithm and improve existential bounds.
AI.method: The paper applies a novel Brascamp–Lieb-type inequality in the MDS setting to derive existential bounds and uses MDS codes whose duals admit efficient list decoders for algorithmic results.
AI.result: Achieves satisfaction rate s=1 when R>0.75 (matching average-case bound, vs DQI requiring R=1). Improves existential threshold from R>0.7495 to R>0.7158. Generalizes existential results to Max-LINSAT with arbitrary MDS codes; algorithmic results apply to MDS codes with efficiently list-decodable duals.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first quantum algorithm solving OPI in worst-case beyond DQI regime, improves existing existential bounds, and introduces a novel inequality technique with potential broader applications.

title: Tuning the universality class of a quantum process by Trotterization
summary: We numerically analyze a discretized version of the quantum contact process, a non-equilibrium model having a competition between a coherent infection process and a dissipative recovery process. Previously, the continuous-time version has been discussed to have a phase transition in a novel quantum universality class, while experimental investigations of a related process have pointed towards the transition being in the classical directed percolation class. We demonstrate that these differences stem from details of the discretization of the process and construct a systematic way to continuously interpolate between these results. Finally, we provide evidence that the modification of the universality class is due to destructive interference effects, showing a clear quantum-mechanical origin.

AI.tldr: A discretized quantum contact process is numerically analyzed, revealing that discrepancies between continuous-time (novel quantum class) and experimental (classical directed percolation class) phase transitions arise from discretization details. A continuous interpolation is constructed, and evidence shows destructive interference effects cause the quantum universality class modification.
AI.motivation: To resolve conflicting reports about the universality class of the quantum contact process—continuous-time theory predicts a novel quantum class, while experiments suggest classical directed percolation—and to understand the role of discretization and quantum effects.
AI.method: Numerical analysis of a discretized version of the quantum contact process with a coherent infection process and dissipative recovery, constructing a systematic continuous interpolation between discretization schemes.
AI.result: Differences in phase transition universality classes stem from discretization details; destructive interference effects are identified as the quantum-mechanical origin of the modified universality class.
AI.conclusion: The quantum contact process's universality class is sensitive to discretization, and destructive interference provides a clear quantum origin for the observed deviation from classical directed percolation.

title: Electrons Hopping across a Molecular Network: Spectra and Symmetries
comment: submitted to special issue in Physics: "Quantum Theory 100 Years Later: advances on Foundations and Applications"
summary: We investigate interacting spinless electrons on finite molecular ring networks described by a tight-binding Hubbard Hamiltonian. The interplay between lattice geometry, Coulomb interactions and discrete symmetries is analysed for rings with $L=3,4,5,6$ nodes, filled with one, two or three electrons. Special attention is devoted to the role of the network symmetries in determining the structure of the many-body spectrum and the Mulliken classification of the eigenstates. Using group-theoretical methods, we examine the evolution of the spectra in the presence of an external magnetic flux. The Zeeman effect lifts degeneracies and results in combination with the Coulomb interaction to avoided crossings in symmetry sectors. We identify a qualitatively distinction between systems with an even and odd number of particles. At half-filling, particle-hole symmetry (duality) protects selected symmetry sectors against Zeeman splitting.

AI.tldr: The paper studies interacting spinless electrons on finite molecular ring networks using a tight-binding Hubbard model, analyzing how lattice geometry, Coulomb interactions, and discrete symmetries shape many-body spectra for rings of varying sizes. It uses group theory to examine spectral evolution under magnetic flux, identifies parity-dependent behavior, and finds that particle-hole symmetry at half-filling protects certain sectors from Zeeman splitting.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between lattice geometry, Coulomb interactions, and discrete symmetries in finite molecular ring networks, and to analyze how these factors determine the many-body spectrum and eigenstate classification.
AI.method: Tight-binding Hubbard Hamiltonian with group-theoretical methods; analysis of rings with L=3-6 nodes filled with 1-3 electrons; Mulliken classification of eigenstates; examination of spectral evolution under external magnetic flux (Zeeman effect).
AI.result: Zeeman effect lifts degeneracies and combines with Coulomb interaction to produce avoided crossings in symmetry sectors. A qualitative distinction exists between even and odd particle numbers. At half-filling, particle-hole symmetry (duality) protects selected symmetry sectors against Zeeman splitting.
AI.conclusion: Network symmetries play a crucial role in determining many-body spectral structure; particle-hole symmetry provides protection against Zeeman splitting at half-filling, and there is a fundamental even-odd parity distinction in the system's behavior.

title: High-rate continuous-variable quantum key distribution coexisting with Tb/s coherent classical transmission in hollow-core fiber
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) can provide secret keys with security rooted in quantum mechanics, but operation alongside high-capacity classical traffic remains limited by the excess-noise budget of weak quantum states in conventional solid-core fiber. Here, we combine ultralow-loss anti-resonant hollow-core fiber with residual-carrier-assisted discrete-modulation continuous-variable QKD (DM-CV-QKD) to address both propagation-induced coexistence noise and low-SNR phase recovery. Over a 24.3-km hollow-core link with 3.3-dB end-to-end loss, a dual-polarization 15-Gbaud DM-CV-QKD channel achieves an average asymptotic secret-key rate (SKR) of 153.22 Mb/s and a finite-size SKR of 149.99 Mb/s, while 39 coherent wavelength-division-multiplexed channels deliver an aggregate data rate of 7.6 Tb/s and a net data rate of 7.2 Tb/s. The system can even sustain a positive SKR under a high classical launch power of up to 15 dBm, without an optical bandpass filter (BPF). Finite-size analysis against collective attacks further yields a projected positive secret-key rate at a 100-km-equivalent condition. These results show that an anti-resonant hollow-core fiber, combined with carrier-assisted phase recovery, can greatly extend the operating regime of shared-fiber quantum-secured coherent links, pointing to a promising approach for integrating high-rate CV-QKD with high-capacity optical networks.

AI.tldr: A 24.3-km hollow-core fiber link combining anti-resonant fiber with discrete-modulation CV-QKD achieves 153 Mb/s asymptotic secret-key rate alongside 7.2 Tb/s classical data traffic over 39 WDM channels, demonstrating coexistence without optical bandpass filtering and projecting positive key rates at 100-km-equivalent conditions.
AI.motivation: Conventional solid-core fiber limits quantum-classical coexistence due to excess noise from high-power classical signals overwhelming weak quantum states; this work aims to overcome that noise bottleneck using hollow-core fiber and carrier-assisted phase recovery.
AI.method: Ultralow-loss anti-resonant hollow-core fiber is combined with residual-carrier-assisted discrete-modulation continuous-variable QKD (DM-CV-QKD) and a dual-polarization 15-Gbaud setup over a 24.3-km link with 3.3-dB end-to-end loss.
AI.result: Average asymptotic SKR of 153.22 Mb/s, finite-size SKR of 149.99 Mb/s, classical aggregate data rate of 7.6 Tb/s (net 7.2 Tb/s) from 39 WDM channels, positive SKR sustained at up to 15 dBm classical launch power without optical BPF, and projected positive SKR at 100-km-equivalent condition.
AI.conclusion: Anti-resonant hollow-core fiber combined with carrier-assisted phase recovery significantly extends the operating regime for shared-fiber quantum-secured coherent links, offering a promising path for integrating high-rate CV-QKD with high-capacity classical optical networks.

title: Moment Optimization in the Navascués-Pironio-Acín Hierarchy
summary:
The Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy provides a convergent sequence of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations for noncommutative polynomial optimisation, ubiquitous in quantum physics. However, its practical applicability is limited by the combinatorial growth in operator moments required at each level. Since not all moments contribute equally to bound tightness, selecting moments within a fixed computational budget is a relevant problem.
  We reframe moment selection as combinatorial subset selection and show it is governed by strong higher-order synergistic interactions among moments, quantified through a marginal synergy diagnostic adapted from complex systems theory. We develop and compare three optimisation methods: Parallel Tempering (PT), an RBM-based reinforcement learning policy, and Bayesian Optimisation (BO). On the $I_{3322}$ Bell inequality benchmark, all three substantially outperform greedy approaches at costs around two orders of magnitude below brute force, with the RBM achieving the closest approach to optimal throughout the hard transition regime.
  We apply the framework to the 174 Bell inequalities in the $(4,4,2,2)$ scenario, finding heterogeneous convergence behaviour across inequalities, and to the one-dimensional Heisenberg spin chain, demonstrating that physically motivated monomial bases are internally compressible and are not globally optimal in general. A budget-aware search over a broader pool improves certified bounds on long-range correlations by nearly two orders of magnitude. These results establish a scalable framework for moment selection in noncommutative polynomial optimisation, with broad applications across quantum physics and quantum information.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes moment selection in the NPA hierarchy as a combinatorial subset selection problem, revealing strong higher-order synergistic interactions among moments. Three optimization methods (Parallel Tempering, RBM-based reinforcement learning, Bayesian Optimisation) outperform greedy approaches, with RBM achieving closest-to-optimal. Applied to Bell inequalities and Heisenberg spin chain, the framework finds physically motivated bases are not globally optimal and budget-aware search improves certified bounds by nearly two orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: The NPA hierarchy is crucial for noncommutative polynomial optimisation in quantum physics, but its practical use is limited by combinatorial growth in operator moments. Since not all moments contribute equally to bound tightness, selecting moments within a fixed computational budget is a relevant but unsolved problem.
AI.method: Reframes moment selection as combinatorial subset selection governed by higher-order synergistic interactions quantified via a marginal synergy diagnostic adapted from complex systems theory. Develops three optimization methods: Parallel Tempering (PT), RBM-based reinforcement learning policy, and Bayesian Optimisation (BO).
AI.result: All three methods substantially outperform greedy approaches at ~100x lower cost than brute force. RBM achieves closest to optimal through the hard transition regime. Applied to 174 Bell inequalities in (4,4,2,2) scenario showing heterogeneous convergence, and to 1D Heisenberg spin chain showing physically motivated bases are compressible and not globally optimal. Budget-aware search improves long-range correlation bounds by ~100x.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a scalable framework for moment selection in noncommutative polynomial optimisation with broad applications across quantum physics and quantum information.

title: Robustness of periodicity in Grover walks under a magnetic vector potential
summary: We study the effect of magnetic vector potentials on periodic Grover walks on finite graphs. The magnetic vector potential is introduced through the framework of quantum graphs, which induces the Grover walk as a special case. We regard the vector potential as a perturbation of a periodic Grover walk and investigate the robustness of its periodicity. Our analysis reveals that the response to such perturbations depends on the spectral structure of the underlying graph. In particular, when the graph possesses at least one non-simple eigenvalue, we derive a Hermitian matrix that characterizes the robustness of its periodicity. As a consequence, we show that the perturbed dynamics is asymptotically described by a continuous-time quantum walk generated by this Hermitian matrix.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how magnetic vector potentials affect periodic Grover walks on finite graphs, finding that the robustness of periodicity under such perturbations depends on the spectral structure of the graph. When the graph has at least one non-simple eigenvalue, a Hermitian matrix characterizes robustness, and the perturbed dynamics asymptotically becomes a continuous-time quantum walk generated by this matrix.
AI.motivation: To understand how magnetic vector potentials perturb the periodicity of Grover walks on finite graphs and to characterize the conditions under which periodicity is robust or breaks down.
AI.method: Magnetic vector potentials are introduced via the framework of quantum graphs, treating them as perturbations of periodic Grover walks. The analysis focuses on spectral properties of the underlying graph, particularly non-simple eigenvalues, to derive a Hermitian matrix that governs the perturbed dynamics.
AI.result: The response to magnetic perturbations depends on the spectral structure of the graph. For graphs with at least one non-simple eigenvalue, a Hermitian matrix is derived that characterizes the robustness of periodicity.
AI.conclusion: The perturbed Grover walk dynamics asymptotically converges to a continuous-time quantum walk generated by the derived Hermitian matrix, linking discrete-time and continuous-time quantum walks under magnetic perturbations.

title: Quantum Remote Implementation of Hybrid Operations on Hyperstates Using Hyperentangled States
summary: Quantum remote control, also known as quantum remote implementation of an operator (QRIO), enables the remote manipulation of an arbitrary quantum state by implementing a desired quantum operation at a distant location. Significant progress has recently been made in developing QRIO protocols and their variants. Most existing schemes employ hyperentangled states where entanglement is shared across multiple degrees of freedom (DOFs). However, these protocols typically exploit only one degree of freedom at a time. In this work, we propose a QRIO protocol that simultaneously utilizes the polarization and spatial DOFs of a two-qubit hyperentangled state to remotely implement an arbitrary hybrid operator on an unknown single-photon two-qubit hyperstate. The shared hyperentangled resource is realized using the polarization and spatial modes of photons, while the protocol is constructed using linear optical elements and cross-Kerr nonlinear interactions to facilitate effective photon-photon coupling. Furthermore, the effects of measurement errors arising from finite coherent state distinguishability and coherent state dissipation are analyzed and the corresponding success probability of the protocol is evaluated. The results demonstrate that an appropriate choice of the cross-Kerr phase shift and coherent state amplitude significantly enhances the protocol performance, making the proposed scheme a promising candidate for hybrid quantum communication and distributed quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum remote control (QRIO) protocol that simultaneously uses both polarization and spatial degrees of freedom of a two-qubit hyperentangled state to remotely implement an arbitrary hybrid operator on an unknown single-photon two-qubit hyperstate, using linear optics and cross-Kerr nonlinear interactions, with analysis of measurement errors and success probability.
AI.motivation: Existing QRIO protocols exploit only one degree of freedom at a time despite using hyperentangled states shared across multiple DOFs, limiting their efficiency. This work aims to simultaneously utilize both polarization and spatial DOFs to enable remote implementation of an arbitrary hybrid operator.
AI.method: The protocol employs a two-qubit hyperentangled state shared via polarization and spatial modes of photons, constructed using linear optical elements and cross-Kerr nonlinear interactions for photon-photon coupling. The effects of measurement errors from finite coherent state distinguishability and coherent state dissipation are analyzed, and the success probability is evaluated as a function of cross-Kerr phase shift and coherent state amplitude.
AI.result: An appropriate choice of the cross-Kerr phase shift and coherent state amplitude significantly enhances the protocol performance, making the scheme effective despite measurement errors and dissipation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed protocol is a promising candidate for hybrid quantum communication and distributed quantum information processing by enabling simultaneous exploitation of multiple DOFs in hyperentangled states for remote operator implementation.

title: Binary Gauss Stabilizers for Abelian Lattice Gauge Theories
summary: Gauge theories and quantum error-correcting codes share the same underlying structure: both use constraints to identify a specific subspace of the full Hilbert space. In quantum error correction, these constraints are known as stabilizers, while in gauge theories they correspond to Gauss law. In this work, we consider a family of discrete Abelian lattice gauge theories described by a $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ gauge group with $N$ an arbitrary power of two. In this setting, we find a set of stabilizers for the gauge-invariant subspace which is an alternative to the Gauss operators, and we call them binary Gauss stabilizers. We use this alternative stabilizer group to build practical error-correcting codes exploiting the gauge symmetries of the system without the addition of extra qubits. The applications of our finding are not limited to error correction though. We also provide a new strategy of gauge fixing to remove the redundancies based on our alternative stabilizer, which might provide advantages with respect to already-existing approaches such as the axial gauge. Our results provide new tools to study lattice gauge theories and their quantum simulation, and opens directions for future work at the interface of lattice gauge theory and quantum information.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals a deep connection between gauge theories and quantum error-correcting codes, introducing binary Gauss stabilizers for $\mathbb{Z}_{2^k}$ lattice gauge theories that enable practical error correction without extra qubits and offer a new gauge-fixing strategy.
AI.motivation: To bridge lattice gauge theories and quantum error correction by identifying alternative stabilizer structures (binary Gauss stabilizers) for discrete Abelian gauge groups, enabling practical error-correcting codes and improved gauge-fixing methods.
AI.method: The authors consider discrete Abelian lattice gauge theories with $\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ gauge group (N a power of two), derive binary Gauss stabilizers as an alternative to standard Gauss law operators, and demonstrate how these stabilizers can be used to construct error-correcting codes and implement gauge fixing.
AI.result: A set of binary Gauss stabilizers that characterize the gauge-invariant subspace is found, enabling practical error-correcting codes from gauge symmetries without extra qubits, and a new gauge-fixing strategy is provided that may outperform existing approaches like axial gauge.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes new tools at the interface of lattice gauge theory and quantum information, with implications for quantum simulation of gauge theories and future developments in both fields.

title: Limits on Broadcasting Genuine Multipartite Entanglement in Quantum Networks
comment: 4 pages (double column) + 12 pages (single column), 6 figure; Comments are welcome
summary: We establish operational limits on the broadcasting of genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) in quantum networks. Using a distributed protocol in which each of N parties locally implements optimal 1 $\to$ 2 cloning via beam-splitter interactions, we derive exact expressions for the broadcast fidelity of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ), W states, and Cluster states in a limited setting. We show that the fidelity decays exponentially with system size as [c(R)]$^N$, providing a quantitative expression of multipartite entanglement monogamy in the broadcasting setting, and that both state families share a universal normalisation factor arising from independent post-selection probabilities. Most significantly, we prove a no-go result for simultaneous GME certification: for all reflectivities and all system sizes, the two broadcast copies cannot be simultaneously certified as genuinely multipartite entangled within the standard framework of fidelity-based witnesses. We further check this behaviour for three- and four-party cluster states, finding consistent results that support the generality of the no-go beyond the GHZ and W families. This obstruction arises from the redistribution of multipartite coherence, which both reduces the achievable fidelity and increases the corresponding certification threshold. Our results reveal a fundamental trade-off between the broadcastability of multipartite entanglement and its operational certifiability, and delineate intrinsic limits on entanglement distribution in quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes fundamental limits on broadcasting genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) in quantum networks, showing that broadcast fidelity decays exponentially with system size and proving a no-go result: two broadcast copies cannot be simultaneously certified as genuinely multipartite entangled using fidelity-based witnesses.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental limits and trade-offs involved in distributing genuine multipartite entanglement across quantum networks, specifically regarding the broadcastability and certifiability of GME.
AI.method: The authors consider a distributed protocol where N parties each implement optimal 1→2 cloning via beam-splitter interactions. They derive exact fidelity expressions for GHZ, W, and Cluster states, and analyze broadcast fidelity scaling as [c(R)]^N. They examine simultaneous GME certification using fidelity-based witnesses.
AI.result: Fidelity decays exponentially with system size; both GHZ and W families share a universal normalization factor from independent post-selection. A no-go result is proven: simultaneous GME certification of both broadcast copies is impossible for all reflectivities and system sizes. This behavior extends to cluster states.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental trade-off between broadcastability of multipartite entanglement and its operational certifiability, arising from the redistribution of multipartite coherence. This delineates intrinsic limits on entanglement distribution in quantum networks.

title: A Geometric Theory of Fermion-to-Qubit Encodings
summary: Exact fermion to qubit transformations are conventionally regarded as algorithmic tools that translate many-body Hamiltonians into qubit representations for quantum simulation. Here we show that they also define intrinsic geometric representations whose structure encodes physically meaningful information beyond spectral equivalence. We develop a geometric framework based on weighted hypergraphs and coupling space representations constructed from the Bravyi--Kitaev (BK) and Xia--Bian--Kais (XBK) encodings. Within the BK representation, we introduce a geometric observable that compares the algebraic connectivities of the kinetic and interaction hypergraphs, derive its exact analytical dependence on interaction strength, and uncover two geometric universality classes together with an exact spectral organization originating from the binary tree architecture of the encoding. The complementary XBK representation describes the evolution of encoded Hamiltonians through probability measures in coupling space, where optimal transport quantifies interaction-driven reorganization independently of the spectral analysis. Applications to the Hubbard, spinless tV , single impurity Anderson, and Kitaev models demonstrate that these connectivity and transport based geometric descriptions consistently capture the structural evolution of encoded quantum Hamiltonians across distinct classes of many-body systems. Our results establish hypergraph geometry as a new framework for understanding fermion-to-qubit encodings,revealing that they serve not only as computational mappings but also as geometric representations of quantum many-body Hamiltonians.

AI.tldr: Fermion-to-qubit transformations define intrinsic geometric representations via weighted hypergraphs and coupling spaces, revealing universal classes and structural evolution of encoded Hamiltonians beyond spectral equivalence, applicable to Hubbard, tV, Anderson, and Kitaev models.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that fermion-to-qubit encodings (BK and XBK) encode physically meaningful geometric structure beyond mere computational mappings, and to establish hypergraph geometry as a framework for understanding the structural evolution of quantum many-body Hamiltonians.
AI.method: Developed a geometric framework using weighted hypergraphs and coupling space representations from BK and XBK encodings; introduced a geometric observable comparing algebraic connectivities of kinetic/interaction hypergraphs; derived analytical dependence on interaction strength; used optimal transport in coupling space for the XBK representation.
AI.result: Discovery of two geometric universality classes and exact spectral organization from BK's binary tree architecture; XBK captures interaction-driven reorganization via probability measures; consistent structural evolution across Hubbard, spinless tV, single impurity Anderson, and Kitaev models.
AI.conclusion: Hypergraph geometry provides a new framework for fermion-to-qubit encodings, showing they serve as geometric representations of quantum many-body Hamiltonians, not just computational mappings.

title: Evolution-Level Quantum Optimal Control of Single-Qubit Gates with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Quantum gate design is often represented as pulse optimization, although the physical object that implements a gate is the full controlled evolution generated by the pulse. Here we use physics-informed neural networks to represent single-qubit gate design at this evolution level: the control fields, the Bloch-state trajectories, and the total duration are learned together under the Bloch equation. This changes the optimized object from pulse amplitudes to a differentiable physical process whose structure can be inspected and refined. For rotation gates, the optimized evolutions recover the physical organization expected for bounded single-qubit control, with no prescribed pulse ansatz or duration scan. For a geometric gate, the representation identifies localized bottlenecks in maintaining the geometric condition and turns this diagnosis into feedback, reducing the residual path error while preserving high fidelity. Thus physics-informed learning is used not only to synthesize gates, but also to make optimized quantum controls physically readable, diagnosable, and locally refinable. This process-level view may be especially useful for adapting gates to hardware-specific, task-specific, and locally varying experimental constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper uses physics-informed neural networks to design single-qubit gates at the evolution level, learning control fields, Bloch-state trajectories, and gate duration simultaneously under the Bloch equation. This approach makes the optimized quantum controls physically readable, diagnosable, and locally refinable, demonstrated on rotation gates and geometric gates.
AI.motivation: Traditional quantum gate design optimizes pulse amplitudes, but the physical object implementing a gate is the full controlled evolution. The authors aim to shift optimization from pulse parameters to the differentiable physical process itself, enabling structural inspection and refinement.
AI.method: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are used to represent single-qubit gate design, where control fields, Bloch-state trajectories, and total duration are jointly learned under the Bloch equation constraint. The optimization object is thus a differentiable physical process rather than discrete pulse amplitudes.
AI.result: For rotation gates, the optimized evolutions recover the expected physical organization for bounded single-qubit control without prescribed pulse ansatz or duration scanning. For a geometric gate, the representation identifies localized bottlenecks in maintaining the geometric condition, enabling feedback that reduces residual path error while preserving high fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed learning can synthesize gates while making optimized quantum controls physically readable, diagnosable, and locally refinable. This process-level view may be particularly useful for adapting gates to hardware-specific, task-specific, and locally varying experimental constraints.

title: A Three-Point Continuous-Variable Quantum MacWilliams Identity
comment: 35 pages. Ancillary files: positive-definite certificates for the CP collapse theorem (JSON, N=1 exact-rational and N=2 floating-point) and a stdlib-only exact verification script (anc/)
summary: We construct the three-point continuous-variable (CV) quantum MacWilliams identity, extending the two-point framework of Burchards, and give its closed-form integral kernel. Its configuration space carries a symplectic invariant with no classical counterpart, which encodes the GKP quantization condition and a three-point sign phase. Using the identity, we derive the semidefinite-programming bounds it supports on the dimension of CV quantum error-correcting codes, and we prove, in two collapse theorems, that the three-point apparatus does not improve on the two-point bound. For GKP lattice codes the three-point optimum equals the Burchards two-point linear-programming optimum identically. This is an exact determination of the lattice three-point optimum, so the $E_8$ and Leech magic functions saturate it rather than beat it. For general bosonic codes a completely-positive reformulation bypasses the positivity obstruction that rules out the natural factored-form constructions; the phase-sign condition together with Choi positivity then force the three-point term to vanish. We certify this collapse for radial Choi forms on the first eight Laguerre levels at one mode, and leave the full trace-class cone open. Both collapses have a single cause with no classical analogue, the code projector: it orients the bound correctly but also removes the full positivity that powers the classical three-point improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the two-point CV quantum MacWilliams identity to a three-point version, derives SDP bounds for CV QEC codes, but proves two collapse theorems showing the three-point framework does not improve upon two-point bounds for GKP lattice codes and general bosonic codes.
AI.motivation: To understand whether a three-point generalization of the CV quantum MacWilliams identity can yield tighter bounds on the dimension of CV quantum error-correcting codes, particularly exploring symplectic invariants with no classical analogue and the GKP quantization condition.
AI.method: Constructs the three-point CV quantum MacWilliams identity with closed-form integral kernel; applies semidefinite programming to derive bounds; proves collapse theorems for GKP lattice codes (where three-point optimum equals two-point LP optimum) and general bosonic codes (where CP reformulation forces three-point term to vanish); certifies collapse via radial Choi forms on first eight Laguerre levels.
AI.result: The three-point apparatus does not improve on the two-point bound in two collapse theorems. For GKP lattice codes, three-point optimum equals Burchards two-point LP optimum identically. For general bosonic codes, the phase-sign condition and Choi positivity force the three-point term to vanish.
AI.conclusion: Both collapses stem from a single cause with no classical analogue: the code projector orients the bound correctly but removes the full positivity that powers classical three-point improvement.

title: Strong $O$-valued contextuality: ruling out discrete nondeterministic alternatives to quantum theory
summary: Gleason's theorem identifies the Born rule via non-contextuality over an infinite continuous lattice of projectors, while its corollary the Kochen-Specker (KS) theorem rules out the specific class of deterministic ($\{0,1\}$-valued) noncontextual models using finite sets of projectors. Gleason's theorem also indicates the existence of KS-type finite vector constructions to rule out other discrete nondeterministic alternatives to quantum theory beyond the $\{0, 1\}$ case. Here, we construct finite measurement configurations to rule out noncontextual empirical models with outcome probabilities drawn from an arbitrary finite subset $O \subset [0,1]$. We do this by two means: (i) constructing a family of experimentally feasible state-dependent Hardy-type tests, and (ii) proving a generalized KS theorem for a broad class of $O$ that includes prior results as special cases. In the sheaf-theoretic framework of Abramsky and Brandenburger, a hierarchy of probabilistic-possibilistic-strong contextuality has been established quantifying contextuality as a resource. We extend this framework by introducing strong $O$-valued contextuality, showing that quantum theory evades global sections of all finite-valued presheaves. We also discuss the implications of the result on finite many-valued logics as viable ontological models for quantum theory and for contextuality-based (semi)-device-independent protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes Kochen-Specker-type contextuality proofs to rule out noncontextual models with outcome probabilities from any finite subset of [0,1], using Hardy-type tests and a generalized KS theorem, and extends the sheaf-theoretic framework to strong O-valued contextuality.
AI.motivation: To extend Gleason-type and Kochen-Specker-type contextuality results beyond deterministic (0,1-valued) and full probabilistic models, by ruling out noncontextual empirical models where outcome probabilities are drawn from an arbitrary finite subset O of [0,1].
AI.method: (i) Constructing a family of experimentally feasible state-dependent Hardy-type tests; (ii) Proving a generalized KS theorem for a broad class of finite outcome probability sets O; (iii) Extending the sheaf-theoretic framework of Abramsky and Brandenburger to introduce strong O-valued contextuality.
AI.result: Quantum theory evades global sections of all finite-valued presheaves; finite measurement configurations can rule out noncontextual empirical models with outcome probabilities from any finite subset O ⊂ [0,1]; prior results (0,1-valued and full [0,1]-valued) are recovered as special cases.
AI.conclusion: The results rule out finite many-valued logics as viable ontological models for quantum theory and have implications for contextuality-based (semi)-device-independent protocols.

title: Pareto-optimal work extraction and the thermodynamic cost of precision in quantum information engines
summary: We study a finite-time quantum information engine in which a two-level system is measured by a quantum harmonic oscillator acting as a meter and where useful work is extracted conditionally on the measurement outcome. Using multi-objective optimisation, we find a Pareto-optimal trade-off between extractable work and its fluctuations and show that reducing fluctuations entails higher thermodynamic costs: greater information consumption, more engine cycles, longer operation time, and reduced average work output. In the limit of a highly accurate meter, we obtain the work distribution, its moments, and the Pareto front analytically. In this regime, the work statistics of the engine reduce to those of a qubit in contact with a single thermal bath. We further analyse the associated information flows by examining the mutual information and Fisher information, and show that the Pareto-optimal engine designs lie very close to local maxima of the latter with respect to the operation time of the device. Our results provide a compact description of the trade-offs between work, its fluctuations, and thermodynamic costs in quantum information engines.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a finite-time quantum information engine where a two-level system is measured by a quantum harmonic oscillator, finding a Pareto-optimal trade-off between extractable work and its fluctuations, with analytical results derived in the high-accuracy meter limit.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify the fundamental trade-offs between work extraction, fluctuations, and thermodynamic costs in quantum information engines operating under finite-time conditions.
AI.method: Multi-objective optimization is used to find Pareto-optimal trade-offs. Analytical derivations of work distribution, moments, and Pareto front are obtained in the highly accurate meter limit. Information flows are analyzed via mutual information and Fisher information.
AI.result: Reducing work fluctuations requires higher thermodynamic costs: greater information consumption, more engine cycles, longer operation time, and reduced average work output. In the high-accuracy limit, work statistics reduce to those of a qubit coupled to a single thermal bath. Pareto-optimal designs lie near local maxima of Fisher information with respect to operation time.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a compact description of the trade-offs between work, its fluctuations, and thermodynamic costs in quantum information engines, linking optimal design to information-theoretic quantities like Fisher information.

title: Implicit differentiation of tensor network algorithms
summary: The current leading approach to the variational optimization of projected entangled-pair states (PEPS) is based on automatic differentiation, which allows for a convenient evaluation of the energy gradient with respect to the local variational degrees of freedom. However, evaluating the energy gradient not only remains a major computational bottleneck of the optimization procedure, but also suffers from frequent numerical instabilities. In this work, we adopt recent advances in implicit differentiation techniques to address these challenges in PEPS optimization. By reformulating the core step of the gradient computation in terms of a single characteristic equation for the contraction environment, we reduce the cost of the gradient computation and improve its scaling with the problem size. By choosing a suitable parametrization of this characteristic equation based on the intrinsic symmetries of the contraction environment, we can directly remove instabilities from the global gradient computation that would otherwise arise from the derivatives of subroutines of the contraction algorithm. Finally, we demonstrate how this approach drastically simplifies the practical implementation of stable gradient-based PEPS optimization.

AI.tldr: A new implicit differentiation method for PEPS optimization reduces computational cost, improves scaling, and eliminates numerical instabilities by reformulating gradient computation via a single characteristic equation with symmetry-based parametrization.
AI.motivation: Current automatic differentiation for PEPS optimization suffers from high computational cost and frequent numerical instabilities. The goal is to develop a more efficient and stable approach for variational optimization of PEPS.
AI.method: Adopts implicit differentiation techniques. Reformulates gradient computation as a single characteristic equation for the contraction environment. Uses a parametrization based on intrinsic symmetries of the contraction environment to remove instabilities from subroutines of the contraction algorithm.
AI.result: Reduced cost of gradient computation and improved scaling with problem size. Direct removal of numerical instabilities from global gradient computation. Simplified practical implementation of stable gradient-based PEPS optimization.
AI.conclusion: Implicit differentiation with symmetry-based parametrization provides a more efficient, stable, and simpler alternative to automatic differentiation for PEPS optimization, addressing both computational and numerical challenges.

title: Machine-Learning-Empowered Quantum Sensing of the Plaquette Phase in a Three-Level Delta System
summary: We propose a machine-learning-empowered approach to the quantum sensing of the plaquette phase, a gauge-invariant quantity arising in three-level $Δ$ systems. This phase profoundly affects the system dynamics, breaking coherent population trapping and inducing a non-trivial phase dependence of the dynamics. We demonstrate that a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), trained in a supervised-learning framework, can accurately estimate the plaquette phase from STImulated Raman Adiabatic Passage (STIRAP) population transfer efficiencies measured under different driving conditions, which provide experimentally accessible observables. Our results highlight how the combination of coherent control and machine learning (ML) enables effective phase identification in closed-loop quantum systems, opening new perspectives for quantum technologies, specifically quantum sensing applications including synthetic gauge fields.

AI.tldr: A supervised multi-layer perceptron trained on STIRAP population transfer efficiencies can accurately estimate the plaquette phase (a gauge-invariant quantity in three-level Δ systems), demonstrating ML-enhanced quantum sensing for phase identification in closed-loop quantum systems with applications to synthetic gauge fields.
AI.motivation: The plaquette phase is a gauge-invariant quantity in three-level Δ systems that profoundly affects system dynamics (breaking coherent population trapping and inducing non-trivial phase dependence), yet it is not directly accessible experimentally. The authors aim to develop a method to accurately estimate this phase from experimentally measurable observables.
AI.method: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is trained in a supervised-learning framework using STIRAP population transfer efficiencies measured under different driving conditions as input features. The MLP learns to map these experimentally accessible observables to the underlying plaquette phase.
AI.result: The MLP can accurately estimate the plaquette phase from the population transfer efficiency data, demonstrating that machine learning combined with coherent control enables effective phase identification in closed-loop quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: The combination of coherent control and machine learning opens new perspectives for quantum technologies, particularly quantum sensing applications including synthetic gauge fields.

title: Towards logical entanglement creation in trivalent planar architectures
summary: Low-overhead quantum error-correction schemes are essential for enabling quantum computation on registers containing multiple logical qubits. For planar architectures with limited nearest-neighbor qubit connectivity, the surface code has emerged as the leading paradigm. Recent theoretical and experimental work has shown that a physical-qubit connectivity of degree three is sufficient to implement fault-tolerant quantum error correction. In this work, we study lattice surgery in the context of such trivalent architectures and introduce scalable circuit constructions to implement it. Compared with the four-valent measurement scheme, the trivalent lattice-surgery protocol reduces the required resources by $\mathcal{O}(d)$ qubits out of a total qubit count of $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ and by $\mathcal{O}(d)$ two-qubit gates out of a total two-qubit gate count of $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$. We benchmark the logical fidelity of both lattice-surgery schemes in terms of experimentally realistic simulations targeting an implementation with a fluxonium qubit based architecture and find a potential improvement of up to $\approx25\%$ for distance-three. These results open a way for scalable planar trivalent qubit architectures to host a surface-code-based logical quantum processor.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a lattice-surgery protocol for trivalent (degree-3 connectivity) planar qubit architectures, reducing qubit resources by O(d) and two-qubit gates by O(d) compared to the standard four-valent scheme, with up to ~25% improvement in logical fidelity for distance-three as demonstrated via simulations targeting fluxonium qubit implementations.
AI.motivation: Low-overhead quantum error correction is essential for scalable quantum computing; the surface code dominates for planar architectures but typically assumes degree-4 connectivity. Recent work shows degree-3 connectivity suffices for fault-tolerant QEC, motivating the need for efficient lattice-surgery protocols tailored to trivalent architectures.
AI.method: The authors develop scalable circuit constructions for lattice surgery on trivalent (degree-3) planar qubit architectures, analyze resource reductions (qubits and two-qubit gates) compared to the four-valent scheme, and perform fidelity benchmarking via experimentally realistic simulations targeting a fluxonium qubit based architecture.
AI.result: The trivalent protocol reduces resources by O(d) qubits (out of O(d²) total) and O(d) two-qubit gates (out of O(d³) total). Simulations show up to ~25% improvement in logical fidelity for distance-three compared to the four-valent scheme.
AI.conclusion: The results open a pathway for scalable planar trivalent qubit architectures to host a surface-code-based logical quantum processor.

title: SQD-Enabled Circuit Compression for Resource-Efficient Quantum Chemistry
comment: Accepted by IEEE/ACM 2026 International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (IEEE/ACM ICCAD 2026)
summary: Subspace Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) recovers ground-state energies by classically diagonalizing a Hamiltonian in the subspace spanned by quantum samples, requiring only bitstrings with sufficient ground-state overlap rather than an accurate variational energy. We reveal and exploit this underexplored robustness property: how much non-Clifford and variational expressivity can be removed from the sampling circuit before SQD accuracy degrades? We answer through two complementary compression techniques: gradient-based operator pruning, which discards low-impact excitation operators, and Clifford rounding, which snaps remaining parameters to the nearest Clifford angle. Both of these techniques can be applied to a VQE ansatz on a qubit-reduced Hamiltonian. A systematic ablation study across 21 molecules shows that median SQD error stays within chemical accuracy even at 50\% compression on both axes, while simulation speedup reaches $33\times$. Hardware validation on 6 molecules on IBM quantum hardware confirms up to $2.8\times$ transpiled-depth reduction with zero loss in SQD accuracy.

AI.tldr: SQD can recover ground-state energies using low-quality quantum samples; two compression methods (operator pruning and Clifford rounding) remove up to 50% of circuit complexity with minimal accuracy loss, achieving 33× simulation speedup and 2.8× depth reduction on hardware.
AI.motivation: To investigate and exploit the underexplored robustness property of Subspace Quantum Diagonalization (SQD), specifically how much non-Clifford and variational expressivity can be removed from the sampling circuit before SQD accuracy degrades.
AI.method: Two complementary compression techniques: (1) gradient-based operator pruning (discards low-impact excitation operators) and (2) Clifford rounding (snaps remaining parameters to nearest Clifford angle). Both applied to a VQE ansatz on a qubit-reduced Hamiltonian. Systematic ablation study across 21 molecules, with hardware validation on 6 molecules using IBM quantum hardware.
AI.result: Median SQD error stays within chemical accuracy even at 50% compression on both axes; simulation speedup reaches 33×; hardware validation shows up to 2.8× transpiled-depth reduction with zero loss in SQD accuracy.
AI.conclusion: SQD exhibits significant robustness to circuit compression, enabling substantial reductions in circuit complexity and simulation time without sacrificing accuracy, validated both in simulation and on quantum hardware.

title: An experimental pathway towards an exact theory of strong coupling
summary: We employ a mathematically equivalent form of the GKLS master equation to arrive at an exact theoretical description of a two-level system strongly coupled to the environment. The framework, while intuitive, shedding light on the physics of the problem, and agreeing with existing results, such as thermalisation to a non-canonical state, is based around three parameters that are unknown outside of the weak coupling regime -- the analogue to the detailed balance relation, and two coupling strength constants. As a way forward, we propose a feasible experimental protocol based on a solid-state electronic quantum dot device, through which the fundamental parameters of the problem can be revealed, which would further the fundamental understanding of strong coupling.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an exact theoretical description of a two-level system strongly coupled to its environment using a mathematically equivalent form of the GKLS master equation. The framework introduces three unknown parameters (analogue to detailed balance relation and two coupling strength constants) and proposes an experimental protocol using a solid-state quantum dot device to reveal these parameters.
AI.motivation: To provide an exact theoretical description of a two-level system strongly coupled to the environment, where standard weak-coupling approaches break down, and to develop a method for determining the unknown parameters in this regime.
AI.method: A mathematically equivalent form of the GKLS master equation is used to derive an exact theoretical framework. Three key parameters are identified: an analogue to the detailed balance relation and two coupling strength constants. A feasible experimental protocol based on a solid-state electronic quantum dot device is proposed.
AI.result: The framework agrees with existing results such as thermalisation to a non-canonical state. The proposed experimental protocol can reveal the fundamental parameters of strong coupling.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an intuitive, exact description of strong coupling and offers a practical experimental pathway to determine the unknown parameters, advancing fundamental understanding of strong system-environment coupling.

title: Quantum Lock-In Detection via Successive Adiabatic Evolution
summary: In recent years, quantum lock-in detection has emerged as a promising technique to accurately detect weak signals submerged in background noise. However, the signal-to-noise ratio of existing protocols is severely limited by spectral leakage resulting from control operations implemented in pulse form. Here, we propose a general protocol for realizing quantum lock-in detection by employing successive quantum adiabatic evolution. In our protocol, the signal modulation is achieved by adiabatically controlling the time evolution of the quantum probe, which enables the implementation of triangular modulation functions. The realization of triangular-wave modulation fundamentally solves the problem of spectral leakage and facilitates the extraction of the complete characteristics of the target signals. We present a practical implementation scheme of adiabatic quantum lock-in detection based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, and demonstrate that the proposed protocol possesses strong resilience against experimental imperfections. Our results establish adiabatic quantum lock-in detection as a robust and experimentally accessible approach to detection of weak alternating signals in noisy environments, thus promoting the advance of real-world quantum sensing technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum lock-in detection protocol using successive quantum adiabatic evolution with triangular modulation to eliminate spectral leakage, demonstrated on nitrogen-vacancy centers, achieving robust weak signal detection in noisy environments.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum lock-in detection protocols suffer from severely limited signal-to-noise ratio due to spectral leakage caused by pulse-form control operations.
AI.method: A general protocol using successive quantum adiabatic evolution for signal modulation, implementing triangular modulation functions via adiabatic control of the quantum probe's time evolution.
AI.result: Triangular-wave modulation fundamentally solves spectral leakage; the protocol shows strong resilience against experimental imperfections in a nitrogen-vacancy center implementation.
AI.conclusion: Adiabatic quantum lock-in detection is established as a robust and experimentally accessible approach for detecting weak alternating signals in noisy environments, advancing real-world quantum sensing technologies.

title: On the origin of finite entanglement scaling
summary: The concept of finite entanglement scaling forms one of the pillars on which the tensor network ecosystem is built. In this paper, we resolve the open problem of determining the actual perturbations induced by matrix product state approximations of critical systems, and we demonstrate that these can be quite different than the ones predicted by conformal field theory. To that aim, we develop a sparse linear solver to calculate the forward and backward derivatives of 2-dimensional tensor networks with respect to their defining parameters in an implicit way. This algorithm is of independent interest as it provides a primitive for the variational optimization of projected entangled pair states that circumvents the instabilities plaguing traditional automatic differentiation methods.
